metaDescription: Six built-in microwave drawers compared on cabinet cutouts, opening mechanisms, sensor cooking and power, with install checks before you buy.
expertTake: The Frigidaire UMBW2411AS is the best microwave drawer because a known appliance brand, 1000 watts and a quiet push-button drawer make it the safest install. The Midea is the value choice with a child lock and 11 power levels. Anyone who does not need accessible loading should skip drawers and buy a countertop or built-in door model for far less.
introParagraphs: A microwave drawer slides out like a kitchen drawer instead of swinging a door, so you load and unload at waist or counter height. It is a popular choice for islands, under-counter installs and kitchens where lifting hot dishes over a counter edge is a concern.

Drawers cost more than ordinary microwaves and demand a prepared cutout, so fit comes first. After that, the opening mechanism, power, sensor cooking and control placement decide whether the unit is pleasant to use every day. This guide compares the six distinct drawers on those points.

specList.label: Drawer
specList.value: Opens and closes with a button

specList.label: Install

products.description:
Frigidaire builds this drawer around a plain, reliable idea: a 1.2 cubic foot cavity, 1000 watts of power and a drawer that opens and closes at the touch of a button. The motion is smooth and quiet, which matters in an open kitchen. Cooking and defrosting run quickly and evenly at that wattage.

Its main advantage over the other drawers is brand reach. Frigidaire has a wide service network, and a built-in drawer is a hassle to swap if a part fails. The unit is 24 inches wide, a standard cutout width for under-counter and island installs. Compared with the Sharp, you lose the concealed angled control panel but gain a simpler design.

Ownership is simple. Take a cloth to the interior after use, keep the drawer slides free of crumbs and leave the installer's ventilation gaps clear. It is the safest drawer to buy if you value support over features.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a mainstream drawer with a strong service network.
pros: Drawer opens and closes at a button press
Major brand with wide service reach
cons: Costs more than a door-style built-in

products.name: Sharp SMD2470ASY 24 in 1.2 cu ft 950W microwave drawer
products.description:
Sharp was early to the microwave drawer, and this model shows it. The control panel is concealed inside the drawer and opens to a 45 degree angle, so the buttons are easy to read from a standing position. The drawer opens automatically and closes hands-free, which helps when you are holding a hot dish.

Output is 950 watts, slightly below the 1000 watt rivals, so cooking is a touch slower. The 1.2 cubic foot cavity matches the others, and flexible placement lets you set it under a counter or in an island. The concealed panel keeps the front of the cabinet clean and uncluttered.

A concealed panel means you must open the drawer to adjust settings, which some owners find slower. Wipe the panel after steamy cooking, and keep the slides clean. It suits owners who value a seamless look and a well-angled interface. Compared with the Frigidaire, the 50 watt gap is small, and many owners will pick on looks. Check that the angled panel suits the height of the cabinet in your layout.
products.bestFor: Design-minded kitchens that want a concealed control panel.
pros: Concealed panel angles up for easy reading
cons: 950 W is slightly slower than rivals

products.name: Midea 1.2 cu ft 1000W stainless microwave drawer with child lock
products.description:
Midea offers the lowest-cost route into a drawer in this lineup. The body measures about 23.6 inches wide, 23.5 inches deep and 15 inches high, with a 1.2 cubic foot cavity and 1000 watts of output. Eleven power levels and a one-touch start give fine control, and a child lock blocks stray presses.

The design is simple, with a Touch and Go panel that starts cooking with a press. It lacks the polish of the Sharp's concealed panel, and the brand has less service reach than Frigidaire. The listed depth of 23.5 inches means you need a deep cabinet, so check the cutout.

Give the interior a wipe and keep the drawer slides clear. For households that want a drawer without a premium price, this is a sensible pick. Next to the Frigidaire, you give up service reach and some polish while keeping the same 1000 watts. If the cabinet depth is available, the Midea is the lowest-risk way to get an accessible microwave.
products.bestFor: Cost-conscious buyers who want a drawer with a child lock and many power levels.
cons: Deep body needs a deep cabinet

products.name: KoolMore 24 in 1.2 cu ft 1000W stainless microwave drawer
products.description:
KoolMore builds this drawer with a one-touch open and a slow-closing action, so the drawer never slams. It runs on standard 120 volt power at 1000 watts, with ten custom cooking levels. The stainless finish suits a modern kitchen.

The slow close is a welcome detail, since a heavy drawer filled with hot soup should settle gently. A 1.2 cubic foot cavity and 24 inch width match the other drawers. KoolMore is a niche brand, so check the warranty and service path before buying.

Keep the slides clean and wipe the interior. It is a solid mid-priced drawer for owners who like soft-close hardware. Next to the Reserve, it drops the sensor and the black glass finish. For routine reheating by time, the plain model does the same job for less.
products.bestFor: Owners who value soft-close hardware in a mid-priced drawer.
cons: 1.2 cu ft matches rather than beats rivals

products.name: KoolMore Reserve 24 in 1.2 cu ft microwave drawer with electric opening
products.description:
KoolMore Reserve adds sensor cooking and a melt mode to a 24 inch drawer. Electric opening handles the drawer motion, and a black stainless exterior with tempered glass looks sharp in modern kitchens. Ten variable power levels sit on a 1000 watt base.

Interior lighting makes it easy to see food, and a safety lock helps with children. Sensor cooking measures moisture to set time, so reheating needs less guesswork. Compared with the plain KoolMore 24 inch drawer, you gain sensors and a more refined finish.

Keep the glass clean and the slides clear. It suits homeowners who want features and style in a drawer. Tempered glass looks smart but shows fingerprints, so keep a cloth near. The melt mode is handy for butter and chocolate at low settings.
products.bestFor: Modern kitchens that want sensor cooking and a black stainless finish.
pros: Sensor cooking with a melt mode
cons: Carries a higher cost than the plain KoolMore

products.name: KoolMore KM-MD30-SS 30 in 1.2 cu ft stainless microwave drawer
products.description:
This KoolMore is the wider cutout option, a 30 inch drawer for kitchens built around 30 inch cabinets. It keeps the 1.2 cubic foot capacity of the 24 inch models, so the extra width is about fit rather than volume. A top control panel gives easy access to the main functions.

The 30 inch width pairs with wall ovens and cabinet banks that use the same width, which gives a neat built-in column. Like other KoolMore models, it has a smaller service network than Frigidaire. Do not buy it for capacity, since the extra width buys alignment, not room.

Wipe down the interior and keep the slides clear. Pick it when your kitchen design calls for a 30 inch drawer.
products.bestFor: Kitchens designed around a 30 in cabinet column.
pros: 30 in width aligns with wall oven banks
Top control panel is easy to reach
Same 1.2 cu ft capacity as 24 in models
cons: Extra width does not add capacity

buyingCriteria.explanation: Drawers need a precise cutout, and the Midea is listed at about 23.6 inches wide and 23.5 inches deep. A cabinet that is too shallow will block the slides. Confirm the width, height and depth from the installation sheet before you buy. Also leave the required ventilation gaps, because trapped heat shortens the life of the magnetron and the motor. Have the cabinetmaker confirm the floor of the cutout is level and strong, since a drawer full of soup is heavy. Many installation problems come from a cabinet that was cut a few millimeters off.

Most drawers here are 24 inches, and the KoolMore KM-MD30-SS is 30 inches. All keep 1.2 cubic feet of capacity, so extra width buys alignment, not volume. Choose width by your cabinet layout. A 30 inch drawer next to a 30 inch wall oven looks tidier than a 24 inch unit. The extra width does not add volume, so do not pay more for it expecting a bigger cavity. Filler panels can bridge a 24 inch unit into a wider opening if needed.

The Frigidaire opens and closes at a button press, the Sharp opens automatically and closes hands-free, the KoolMore 24 inch has slow closing, and the KoolMore Reserve uses electric opening. Motorized slides add convenience and a part that can fail. Check how the drawer behaves if power is lost, since some can be eased open by hand. Ask whether a replacement motor or control board is stocked, because those are the parts most likely to fail. A smooth action out of the box can feel different after several years of daily loads.

The Frigidaire, Midea and KoolMore models list 1000 watts, while the Sharp lists 950 watts. The KoolMore Reserve adds sensor cooking and a melt mode. For daily use, 1000 watts is the sweet spot, and sensor cooking helps with varied reheats. A drawer's flat tray also means dishes sit on the floor of the cavity rather than on a turntable, so even heating depends on the wave pattern. Stir and rotate dishes by hand halfway through long cooks.

The Sharp conceals its panel inside the drawer at a 45 degree angle, the KoolMore 30 inch uses a top panel, and others use front controls. A concealed panel gives a clean look but needs the drawer open. Choose based on whether you value looks or quick access. If several people use the oven, a visible panel prevents wrong settings. A tilted concealed panel suits one cook who knows the routine.

The Midea and KoolMore Reserve list child or safety locks. A drawer sits at child height, so a lock matters in family homes. Service reach also matters, because a built-in unit is hard to replace. Frigidaire and Sharp have broader networks than the niche brands. Keep the purchase record and installation photos in case a warranty claim is needed. Ask the seller who handles repairs before you buy.

howWeEvaluated.title: Form factor purity
howWeEvaluated.description: We kept only true microwave drawers and left out built-in door models. That left six distinct machines. Finish variants of one model were counted once.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared widths, depths and published cutouts. Five are 24 inches wide and the KoolMore KM-MD30-SS is 30 inches. Fit was weighted above features.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drawer mechanism
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared opening and closing actions from the spec sheets. The Frigidaire, Sharp and KoolMore Reserve are motorized, and the KoolMore 24 inch offers slow closing. Smooth operation was credited.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cooking features
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared power and aids. Five list 1000 W, the Sharp lists 950 W, and the KoolMore Reserve adds sensor cooking. Aids that cut guesswork scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership signals
howWeEvaluated.description: Long-term owner notes lean toward slides, motors and touch pads as wear points. Service reach mattered because a built-in unit is hard to replace.

rows: Sensor cooking and style at the low end

cards.label: Motorized
cards.text: The Frigidaire, Sharp and KoolMore Reserve open and close with a button. They are convenient when your hands are full. They add a motor that can fail.

cards.label: Soft close
cards.text: The KoolMore 24 inch opens at a touch and closes slowly. It is gentle on hot soups. It has fewer extras.

howToChoose.note: Pick motorized for convenience. Pick soft close for gentle motion and simplicity.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Accessible kitchens need loading at waist height, a drawer that moves smoothly and controls that are easy to read. A motorized open and close helps when hands are full.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Frigidaire is the safest pick, and the Sharp adds a readable angled panel. The Midea suits tighter budgets.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want a seamless look or the best service network. The Sharp and Frigidaire earn their cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You just want a drawer that works. The Midea and KoolMore Reserve give 1000 W at a lower cost.

maintenance.why: Leftover splatter takes in energy and can cause hot spots. Wipe while warm.
Crumbs and grease stick the slides. Wipe them with a damp cloth.
Covered vents let heat build up in the cabinet. Clear dust from gaps.
Grease on touch pads causes false presses. Use a dry microfiber cloth.
A lock that does not engage defeats its purpose. Check it per the manual.

faq.q: Are microwave drawers worth the extra cost?
faq.a: They suit accessible kitchens, islands and under-counter installs where lifting hot dishes is a concern. For standard kitchens, a door-style microwave costs far less. Choose a drawer for ergonomics, not for cooking quality, because the heating results match a door unit of the same wattage.

faq.q: Do microwave drawers cook as well as regular ones?
faq.a: Yes. The cooking hardware is the same 1000 watt magnetron design. The difference is the drawer and the cutout.

faq.q: What size cutout does a microwave drawer need?
faq.a: Most are 24 inches wide, and one here is 30 inches. The Midea lists about 23.5 inches deep. Always confirm the installation sheet.

faq.q: Can I put a drawer under the counter?
faq.a: Yes, many are designed for under-counter, island or wall installs. Leave the ventilation gaps the manual calls for. A level, solid base is essential.
Typical service life runs to several years, with slides, motors and touch pads as common failures. Choosing a brand with strong service helps.

faq.q: Do I need a trim kit?
faq.a: Drawers usually install in a cabinet cutout without a trim kit, but check each listing. Some may include finishing parts.
